grep: Searches for specific patterns or text strings within files and outputs matching lines.
cd: Changes the current working directory in the command-line interface.
wget: A non-interactive network downloader used to retrieve files from the web via HTTP, HTTPS, and FTP.
curl: A command-line tool for transferring data to or from a server using various protocols like HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, etc.
ls: Lists directory contents, showing files and folders inside the current working directory.
pwd: Prints the absolute path of the current working directory.
mkdir: Creates a new directory or folder at the specified location.
chmod: Changes file or directory access permissions in Unix-like operating systems.
chown: Changes the user and group ownership of file system files and directories.
iptables: A user-space application program that allows a system administrator to configure the IP packet filter rules of the Linux kernel firewall.
systemctl: A command-line tool to inspect and manage the systemd system and service manager.
linux: A free and open-source Unix-like operating system kernel first released by Linus Torvalds in 1991.
unix: A family of multitasking, multiuser operating systems originally developed at Bell Labs in the 1970s.
kernel: The core of an operating system that manages hardware, memory, processes, and system calls.
shell: A command-line interpreter that provides an interface for users to interact with the operating system.
bash: Bourne Again Shell: the default shell on most Linux distributions and macOS.
zsh: Z shell: an extended Bourne shell with many improvements, popular as an interactive shell.
fish: Friendly Interactive Shell: a user-friendly shell with syntax highlighting and autosuggestions.
environment variable: A named value in a process's environment, used to configure programs at runtime.
path: The environment variable listing directories searched for executable commands.
alias: A shell shortcut that expands to a longer command.
pipe: A shell operator (|) that sends the output of one command as input to another.
redirect: A shell operator that sends command output to a file or device instead of the terminal.
glob: A pattern-matching syntax in shells using wildcards like * and ? to match filenames.
stdin: Standard input: the default input stream for a process, usually the terminal.
stdout: Standard output: the default output stream for a process, usually the terminal.
stderr: Standard error: the stream where a process writes error messages, separate from stdout.
exit code: A number returned by a process to indicate success (0) or failure (non-zero).
sudo: A program that allows a permitted user to execute a command as another user, typically root.
root: The superuser account on Unix-like systems with unrestricted access to the system.
user: A user account on a multi-user operating system, identified by a username and a numeric UID.
group: A collection of users in Unix-like systems, used to grant shared permissions.
permission: An access right on a file or directory, specifying read, write, and execute for user, group, and others.
umask: A value that determines the default permissions for newly created files and directories.
file system: The structure and rules an operating system uses to store and retrieve files on a storage device.
mount: The act of making a file system accessible at a directory in the operating system's tree.
partition: A logical division of a storage device that can hold a file system.
inode: A data structure on Unix-like file systems that stores metadata about a file (not its name).
symlink: A symbolic link: a special file that points to another file or directory.
hard link: A directory entry that points to the same inode as another file, effectively a second name for the same data.
tmpfs: A temporary file system stored in memory (RAM) rather than on persistent storage.
swap: Disk space used as virtual memory when physical RAM is exhausted.
daemon: A background process that runs without a controlling terminal, often providing a service.
process: A running instance of a program, with its own memory, file descriptors, and PID.
pid: Process ID: a numeric identifier assigned to each running process.
signal: A software interrupt delivered to a process to notify it of an event (e.g., SIGTERM, SIGKILL).
job: A process or pipeline managed by a shell's job control system.
cron: A time-based job scheduler on Unix-like systems that runs commands at specified intervals.
journalctl: A command-line tool to view logs collected by the systemd journal.
unit: A systemd configuration file describing a service, socket, device, mount, or other resource.
init: The first process started by the kernel on a Unix-like system, responsible for starting other processes.
init system: The software that initializes the system after the kernel boots and manages services.
bootloader: A program that loads the operating system kernel into memory at boot time.
grub: GRand Unified Bootloader: a widely used bootloader for Linux and other operating systems.
filesystem hierarchy: The standardized directory layout on Unix-like systems (e.g., /etc, /usr, /var).
pacman: The package manager for Arch Linux, used to install, update, and remove software.
aur: Arch User Repository: a community-driven repository of PKGBUILD files for Arch Linux.
pkgbuild: A shell script that describes how to build a package from source, used by makepkg.
makepkg: A script that automates building packages from PKGBUILDs on Arch Linux.
yay: Yet Another Yogurt: a popular AUR helper for Arch Linux written in Go.
paru: A feature-rich AUR helper for Arch Linux written in Rust.
reflector: A tool that retrieves and sorts Arch Linux mirror lists by speed and freshness.
base-devel: A package group on Arch Linux that provides essential tools for building packages from source.
arch wiki: The community-maintained documentation wiki for Arch Linux, widely used across Linux distributions.
apt: The package manager used on Debian and Ubuntu systems.
dpkg: The low-level package manager underlying apt on Debian-based systems.
yum: The legacy package manager for RPM-based distributions, superseded by dnf.
dnf: The modern package manager for Fedora and other RPM-based distributions.
rpm: RPM Package Manager: a package format and tool used by Fedora, RHEL, and SUSE.
snap: A universal package format developed by Canonical for Linux.
flatpak: A universal package format for Linux with sandboxing and per-app dependencies.
appimage: A portable Linux application format that runs without installation.
libalpm: The library used by Arch Linux tools to handle package databases, dependencies, and package transactions.
libalpm backend: The package-management backend library used by pacman and other Arch Linux tools.
binary package: A ready-to-install archive containing compiled files, metadata, and installation information.
Binärpaket: A ready-to-install archive containing compiled files, metadata, and installation information.
package database: A database that records package metadata and which files belong to installed packages.
Paketdatenbank: A database that records package metadata and which files belong to installed packages.
package signing: Applying a cryptographic signature to a package so its origin and integrity can be checked.
Paketsignierung: Applying a cryptographic signature to a package so its origin and integrity can be checked.
source code: Human-readable program instructions from which software can be compiled or interpreted.
Quellcode: Human-readable program instructions from which software can be compiled or interpreted.
dependency resolution: Finding required packages and selecting a compatible installation order before installing software.
Abhängigkeitsauflösung: Finding required packages and selecting a compatible installation order before installing software.
package group: A named collection of related packages that can be installed or removed together.
package archive: A file that bundles a package’s program files and metadata for distribution and installation.
package cache: Local storage where downloaded package archives are kept for reuse or rollback.
partial upgrade: Updating only part of a rolling-release system, which can leave incompatible package versions installed.
mirror list: A list of download servers that host copies of a distribution’s software repositories.
official repository: A software collection maintained by a distribution and used by its package manager.
AUR package: Community-provided build instructions in the Arch User Repository; users build the package locally.
AUR-Paket: Community-provided build instructions in the Arch User Repository; users build the package locally.
build from source: Compile and package software from its source code instead of installing a prebuilt binary.
Aus dem Quellcode bauen: Compile and package software from its source code instead of installing a prebuilt binary.
prebuilt binary: An already compiled executable that can be installed without compiling its source code.
vorgebaute Binärdatei: An already compiled executable that can be installed without compiling its source code.
runtime dependency: Software required while a program is running, rather than only while it is being built.
Laufzeitabhängigkeit: Software required while a program is running, rather than only while it is being built.
command flag: An option added to a command, usually with a dash, to change its behavior.
Befehls-Flag: An option added to a command, usually with a dash, to change its behavior.
configuration file: A text file containing settings that control how a program or system behaves.
Konfigurationsdatei: A text file containing settings that control how a program or system behaves.
pactree: A pacman-contrib command that displays a package’s dependency tree.
checkupdates: A pacman-contrib command that checks for package updates without refreshing the system package database.
vercmp: An Arch Linux utility that compares two package version strings using pacman’s version rules.
yay-bin: An AUR package that provides a prebuilt binary of the yay AUR helper.
AUR-Helper: A tool that automates searching, building, and installing packages from the Arch User Repository.
AUR tab completion: Shell completion that suggests AUR package names as a command is typed.
AUR-Tab-Vervollständigung: Shell-Vervollständigung, die beim Tippen eines Befehls Paketnamen aus dem AUR vorschlägt.
pacman wrapper: A program that calls pacman and adds commands or features while retaining its package-management behavior.
pacman-Wrapper: Programm, das pacman aufruft und Befehle oder Funktionen ergänzt, während dessen Paketverwaltung erhalten bleibt.
dependency: A package or library that another program needs to build or run.
package repository: A server or collection of servers that provides packages and metadata to a package manager.
cache directory: A directory where downloaded package files are stored temporarily for reuse.
keyring: A store of trusted public keys used to verify signed packages and repository data.
command-line option: A value or switch passed to a command to select an action or adjust its behavior.
repository synchronization: Refreshing local package metadata from configured software repositories.
system upgrade: Updating installed packages to newer versions available from configured repositories.
package signature: A cryptographic value used to verify that a package was signed by a trusted publisher and was not altered.
signing key: A cryptographic key used to create or verify digital signatures.
.pacsave: A file extension pacman uses for a package configuration file that was modified before removal.
pacman-contrib: A collection of extra Arch Linux package-management tools, including pactree and checkupdates.
package transaction: A package-manager operation that installs, upgrades, or removes packages and updates its database.
package file list: The list of filesystem paths owned by an installed package.
file ownership: The association between an installed file and the package that installed it.
explicitly installed package: A package deliberately requested by the user, rather than installed only as a dependency.
foreign package: An installed package that is not found in the configured official repositories, often because it came from the AUR.
orphan package: A package installed only as a dependency that is no longer required by another installed package.
make-only dependency: A package needed to build software but not needed to run the finished program.
package manager frontend: The user-facing command-line or graphical tool that sends package operations to a backend.
package-manager frontend: The user-facing command-line or graphical tool that sends package operations to a backend.
sync database: The local package metadata database synchronized with configured repositories.
package operation: An action such as searching, installing, querying, upgrading, or removing a package.
package query: A request to inspect installed packages or package information without changing installed software.
dependency tree: A tree-shaped view showing which packages depend on other packages.
version comparison: Comparing package version strings according to a package manager’s version rules.
clone: Create a local copy of a Git repository, including its tracked files and history.
Git clone: The Git operation that copies a remote repository to the local machine.
shell completion: A shell feature that suggests or fills command names, options, or arguments while typing.
repository metadata: Information describing available packages, versions, dependencies, and download locations in a repository.
package source: The repository or origin from which a package is obtained, such as an official repository or the AUR.
package signing key: A key used to verify the signature on a package or repository database.
system package database: Local records of package versions and metadata used by a package manager.
release upgrade: Updating a distribution by installing newer package versions from its repositories.
distribution repository: A maintained collection of packages published for a Linux distribution.
Pakettransaktion: A package-manager operation that installs, upgrades, or removes packages and updates its database.
Dateibesitz: The association between an installed file and the package that installed it.
Fremdpaket: Installiertes Paket, das in den eingerichteten offiziellen Repositories nicht gefunden wird, häufig aus dem AUR.
verwaistes Paket: Nur als Abhängigkeit installiertes Paket, das von keinem anderen installierten Paket mehr benötigt wird.
Build-Abhängigkeit: A package needed to build software but not needed to run the finished program.
Paketabfrage: A request to inspect installed packages or package information without changing installed software.
Abhängigkeitsbaum: Baumförmige Darstellung der Abhängigkeiten zwischen Paketen.
Versionsvergleich: Vergleich von Paketversionsangaben nach den Versionsregeln eines Paketmanagers.
Shell-Vervollständigung: Shell-Funktion, die beim Tippen Befehle, Optionen oder Argumente vorschlägt oder vervollständigt.
Repository-Metadaten: Informationen über verfügbare Pakete, Versionen, Abhängigkeiten und Downloadorte eines Repositories.
Paketquelle: Repository oder Herkunft, aus dem ein Paket bezogen wird, etwa ein offizielles Repository oder das AUR.
Paket-Signaturschlüssel: A key used to verify the signature on a package or repository database.
Repository-Synchronisierung: Aktualisieren lokaler Paketmetadaten aus den eingerichteten Software-Repositories.
Paketmanager-Frontend: Für Benutzer sichtbares Kommandozeilen- oder Grafikwerkzeug, das Paketvorgänge an ein Backend weitergibt.
-S: pacman operation to synchronize package data or install packages from a repository.
-Ss: Search synchronized remote package repositories in pacman.
-Qs: Search the locally installed packages with pacman.
-Sy: Refresh the local package database from repositories without upgrading installed packages.
-Syu: Refresh package databases and upgrade all installed packages; the usual full-system update.
-Qu: List installed packages for which repository updates are available.
-R: Remove an installed package with pacman.
-Rs: Remove a package and dependencies that are no longer required.
-Rns: Remove a package, its unneeded dependencies, and its saved configuration files.
-Q: Query the local package database for installed packages.
-Qe: List packages explicitly installed by the user.
-Qm: List installed packages that are not present in synchronized repositories.
-Qtdq: List dependency packages that are no longer required, in a format suitable for scripts.
--needed: Skip installing a package that is already up to date.
--noconfirm: Run a package operation without interactive confirmation prompts.
-si: makepkg flags that resolve dependencies and install the package after building it.
-Sua: Upgrade AUR packages without upgrading packages from official repositories.
-Qua: List available updates for installed AUR packages.
--devel: Check development packages, often built from version-control repositories, for newer commits.
-Gp: Print a package’s PKGBUILD instead of building or installing it.
-Yc: Remove dependencies that were installed for other packages but are no longer required.
-Scc: Clear cached package archives from pacman’s local cache.
package manager: Software that installs, upgrades, queries, and removes packages while tracking dependencies.
package management: The process of installing, updating, configuring, and removing software packages.
metadata: Descriptive data about other data; package metadata includes its name, version, dependencies, and files.
package metadata: Information about a package, such as its version, dependencies, description, and installation files.
PKGBUILDs: Plural of PKGBUILD: Arch Linux build scripts that describe how to create packages from source.
repo: Informal short form of repository: a collection of software packages and metadata.
repos: Informal short form of repositories: collections of software packages and metadata.
repository: A maintained collection of packages and metadata that a package manager can search and install from.
repositories: Maintained collections of packages and metadata that a package manager can search and install from.
Paketmanager: Software that installs, upgrades, queries, and removes packages while tracking dependencies.
Metadaten: Descriptive data about other data; package metadata includes name, version, dependencies, and files.
Paketmetadaten: Information about a package, such as its version, dependencies, description, and files.
PKGBUILD-Dateien: Arch Linux build scripts that describe how to create packages from source.
Repositorys: Maintained collections of packages and metadata that a package manager can search and install from.
Paketverwaltung: The process of installing, updating, configuring, and removing software packages.
package: An installable archive containing an application or library, metadata, and installation information.
packages: Installable archives containing applications or libraries, metadata, and installation information.
Paket: An installable archive containing an application or library, metadata, and installation information.
Pakete: Installable archives containing applications or libraries, metadata, and installation information.
Repo: Informal short form of repository: a collection of software packages and metadata.
Repos: Informal short form of repositories: collections of packages and metadata.
